Q9191525.summary: Christ stands at the right, larger than his companion, holding a jewelled Gospel book and resting his right arm around the shoulder of Abbot Mena, who holds a scroll and raises his hand. Both have large, wide eyes and golden haloes against an orange sky above green hills; the Greek inscriptions name Christ as 'Saviour' and his companion as 'Apa Mena, the superior'. This rare panel from the monastery of Bawit in Egypt is a moving image of Christ as the companion and protector of the faithful.
facts: The icon was found in 1902 at the monastery of Bawit in Middle Egypt; the Louvre records that it was stolen from the excavation site, bought by Lecomte du Nouÿ and given by him to the museum in 1918.
The Louvre dates it to the 8th century and identifies the wood as sycamore fig, painted in encaustic (beeswax) and tempera; it measures about 58.5 × 57.7 cm.
Wikipedia reads Christ's hand resting on Mena's far shoulder as a sign of his protective authority over the abbot; the abbot is shown slightly smaller than Christ.

links.label: Wikipedia: Icon of Christ and Abbot Mena

Q9191525.notes: Dating differs: the Louvre gives 8th century (700–799); English Wikipedia says second half of the 6th century. The Louvre date is used. The Louvre currently lists it as not on display.

cur:objects-kells-south-cross.summary: At the centre of the weathered head on the west face of this cross Christ is shown crucified, his arms outstretched along the arms of the cross, with figures pressing in from either side. The cross is dedicated by its inscription to Saints Patrick and Columba, the patrons of Irish Christianity and of the Columban monastery of Kells. Though worn, the carving still conveys the Irish devotion to Christ crucified at the heart of the monastic enclosure.
facts: It is the oldest of the five high crosses at Kells and bears an inscription naming Saints Patrick and Columba, from which it takes its alternative name (photographer's documentation).
Wikipedia notes that the round tower and high crosses at Kells are a National Monument of Ireland.
cur:objects-kells-south-cross.notes: The image is a weathered close view from below; the identification of the central figure as the crucified Christ follows the usual west-face scheme but the photograph is not sharp.
